entries.6c87b6bd81238461602c3c50328975ed86af3b52: <div sID="gen11912" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="79" osisID="Ps.79" sID="Ps.79"/> <div eID="gen11912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11913" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11914" type="x-p"/> This psalm, if penned with any particular event in view, is with most probability made to refer to the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, and the woeful havoc made of the Jewish nation by the Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar. It is set to the same tune, as I may say, with the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and that weeping prophet borrows two verses out of it (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.6-Ps.79.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>) and makes use of them in his prayer, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.25">Jer. x. 25</reference>. Some think it was penned long before by the spirit of prophecy, prepared for the use of the church in that cloudy and dark day. Others think that it was penned then by the spirit of prayer, either by a prophet named Asaph or by some other prophet for the sons of Asaph. Whatever the particular occasion was, we have here, I. A representation of the very deplorable condition that the people of God were in at this time, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.1-Ps.79.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. A petition to God for succour and relief, that their enemies might be reckoned with (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.6-Ps.79.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.10">10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.12">12</reference>), that their sins might be pardoned (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.8-Ps.79.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>), and that they might be delivered, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.11">ver. 11</reference>. III. A plea taken from the readiness of his people to praise him, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.13">ver. 13</reference>. In times of the church's peace and prosperity this psalm may, in the singing of it, give us occasion to bless God that we are not thus trampled on and insulted. But it is especially seasonable in a day of treading down and perplexity, for the exciting of our desires towards God and the encouragement of our faith in him as the church's patron.
entries.817e6d5610c9bae38d57d59e50f285e093373655: <div eID="gen11914" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11913" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Mournful Complaints.</title> <div sID="gen11915" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps. <hi type="super">2</hi> The dead bodies of thy servants have they given <hi type="italic">to be</hi> meat unto the fowls of the heaven, the flesh of thy saints unto the beasts of the earth. <hi type="super">3</hi> Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and <hi type="italic">there was</hi> none to bury <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">4</hi> We are become a reproach to our neighbours, a scorn and derision to them that are round about us. <hi type="super">5</hi> How long, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? wilt thou be angry for ever? shall thy jealousy burn like fire? <div eID="gen11915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11916" type="x-p"/> We have here a sad complaint exhibited in the court of heaven. The world is full of complaints, and so is the church too, for it suffers, not only with it, but from it, as <hi type="italic">a lily among thorns.</hi> God is complained to; whither should children go with their grievances, but to their father, to such a father as is able and willing to help? The heathen are complained of, who, being themselves aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, were sworn enemies to it. Though they knew not God, nor owned him, yet, God having them in chain, the church very fitly appeals to him against them; for he is King of nations, to overrule them, to judge among the heathen, and King of saints, to favour and protect them. <div eID="gen11916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11917" type="x-p"/> I. They complain here of the anger of their enemies and the outrageous fury of the oppressor, exerted, <div eID="gen11917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11918" type="x-p"/> 1. Against places, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.1">v. 1</reference>. They did all the mischief they could, (1.) To the holy land; they invaded that, and made inroads into it: "<hi type="italic">The heathen have come into thy inheritance,</hi> to plunder that, and lay it waste." Canaan was dearer to the pious Israelites as it was God's inheritance than as it was their own, as it was the land in which God was known and his name was great rather than as it was the land in which they were bred and born and which they and their ancestors had been long in possession of. Note, Injuries done to religion should grieve us more than even those done to common right, nay, to our own right. We should better bear to see our own inheritance wasted than God's inheritance. This psalmist had mentioned it in the foregoing psalm as an instance of God's great favour to Israel that he had <hi type="italic">cast out the heathen before them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.55">Ps. lxxviii. 55</reference>. But see what a change sin made; now the heathen are suffered to pour in upon them. (2.) To the holy city: <hi type="italic">They have laid Jerusalem on heaps,</hi> heaps of rubbish, such heaps as are raised over graves, so some. The inhabitants were buried in the ruins of their own houses, and their dwelling places became their sepulchres, their long homes. (3.) To the holy house. That sanctuary which God had built like high palaces, and which was thought to be established as the earth, was now laid level with the ground: <hi type="italic">Thy holy temple have they defiled,</hi> by entering into it and laying it waste. God's own people had defiled it by their sins, and therefore God suffered their enemies to defile it by their insolence. <div eID="gen11918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11919" type="x-p"/> 2. Against persons, against the bodies of God's people; and further their malice could not reach. (1.) They were prodigal of their blood, and killed them without mercy; their eye did not spare, nor did they give any quarter (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Their blood have they shed like water,</hi> wherever they met with them, <hi type="italic">round about Jerusalem,</hi> in all the avenues to the city; whoever <hi type="italic">went out or came in</hi> was <hi type="italic">waited for of the sword.</hi> Abundance of human blood was shed, so that the channels of water ran with blood. And they shed it with no more reluctancy or regret than if they had spilt so much water, little thinking that every drop of it will be reckoned for in the day when <hi type="italic">God shall make inquisition for blood.</hi> (2.) They were abusive to their dead bodies. When they had killed them they would let none bury them. Nay, those that were buried, even the <hi type="italic">dead bodies of God's servants, the flesh of his saints,</hi> whose names and memories they had a particular spite at, they dug up again, and <hi type="italic">gave them to be meat to the fowls of the heaven and to the beasts of the earth;</hi> or, at least, they left those so exposed whom they slew; they hung them in chains, which was in a particular manner grievous to the Jews to see, because God had given them an express law against this, as a barbarous thing, <reference osisRef="Deut.21.23">Deut. xxi. 23</reference>. This inhuman usage of Christ's witnesses is foretold (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.9">Rev. xi. 9</reference>), and thus even the dead bodies were witnesses against their persecutors. This is mentioned (says Austin, <hi type="italic">De Civitate Dei, lib.</hi> 1 <hi type="italic">cap.</hi> 12) not as an instance of the misery of the persecuted (for the bodies of the saints shall rise in glory, however they became meat to the birds and the fowls), but of the malice of the persecutors. <div eID="gen11919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11920" type="x-p"/> 3. Against their names (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We that survive have become a reproach to our neighbours;</hi> they all study to abuse us and load us with contempt, and represent us as ridiculous, or odious, or both, upbraiding us with our sins and with our sufferings, or giving the lie to our relation to God and expectations from him; so that we have become <hi type="italic">a scorn and derision to those that are round about us.</hi>" If God's professing people degenerate from what themselves and their fathers were, they must expect to be told of it; and it is well if a just reproach will help to bring us to a true repentance. But it has been the lot of the gospel-Israel to be made unjustly a reproach and derision; the apostles themselves were <hi type="italic">counted as the offscouring of all things.</hi> <div eID="gen11920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11921" type="x-p"/> II. They wonder more at God's anger, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.5">v. 5</reference>. This they discern in the anger of their neighbours, and this they complain most of: <hi type="italic">How long, Lord, wilt thou be angry?</hi> Shall it be <hi type="italic">for ever?</hi> This intimates that they desired no more than that God would be reconciled to them, that his anger might be turned away, and then the remainder of men's wrath would be restrained. Note, Those who desire God's favour as better than life cannot but dread and deprecate his wrath as worse than death.
entries.d633e008ff46b67f0d4699d7a00839dd80c793dd: <div eID="gen11921" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Petitions for Succor and Relief; Petitions for Deliverance.</title> <div sID="gen11922" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Pour out thy wrath upon the heathen that have not known thee, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon thy name. <hi type="super">7</hi> For they have devoured Jacob, and laid waste his dwelling place. <hi type="super">8</hi> O remember not against us former iniquities: let thy tender mercies speedily prevent us: for we are brought very low. <hi type="super">9</hi> Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of thy name: and deliver us, and purge away our sins, for thy name's sake. <hi type="super">10</hi> Wherefore should the heathen say, Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> their God? let him be known among the heathen in our sight <hi type="italic">by</hi> the revenging of the blood of thy servants <hi type="italic">which is</hi> shed. <hi type="super">11</hi> Let the sighing of the prisoner come before thee; according to the greatness of thy power preserve thou those that are appointed to die; <hi type="super">12</hi> And render unto our neighbours sevenfold into their bosom their reproach, wherewith they have reproached thee, O Lord. <hi type="super">13</hi> So we thy people and sheep of thy pasture will give thee thanks for ever: we will show forth thy praise to all generations. <div eID="gen11922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11923" type="x-p"/> The petitions here put up to God are very suitable to the present distresses of the church, and they have pleas to enforce them, interwoven with them, taken mostly from God's honour. <div eID="gen11923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11924" type="x-p"/> I. They pray that God would so turn away his anger from them as to turn it upon those that persecuted and abused them (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Pour out thy wrath,</hi> the full vials of it, <hi type="italic">upon the heathen;</hi> let them wring out the dregs of it, and drink them." This prayer is in effect a prophecy, in which the <hi type="italic">wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men.</hi> Observe here, 1. The character of those he prays against; they are such as have not known God, nor called upon his name. The reason why men do not call upon God is because they do not know him, how able and willing he is to help them. Those that persist in ignorance of God, and neglect of prayer, are the ungodly, who live <hi type="italic">without God in the world.</hi> There are kingdoms that know not God and obey not the gospel, but neither their multitude nor their force united will secure them from his just judgments. 2. Their crime: <hi type="italic">They have devoured Jacob,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.79.7">v. 7</reference>. That is crime enough in the account of him who reckons that those who touch his people touch the apple of his eye. They have not only disturbed, but devoured, Jacob, not only encroached upon his dwelling place, the land of Canaan, but laid it waste by plundering and depopulating it. (3.) Their condemnation: "<hi type="italic">Pour out thy wrath</hi> upon them; do not only restrain them from doing further mischief, but reckon with them for the mischief they have done." <div eID="gen11924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11925" type="x-p"/> II. They pray for the pardon of sin, which they own to be the procuring cause of all their calamities. How unrighteous soever men were, God was righteous in permitting them to do what they did. They pray, 1. That God would not <hi type="italic">remember against them their former iniquities</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.8">v. 8</reference>), either their own former iniquities, that now, when they were old, they might not be made to possess the iniquities of their youth, or the former iniquities of their people, the sins of their ancestors. In the captivity of Babylon former iniquities were brought to account; but God promises not again to do so (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.29-Jer.31.30">Jer. xxxi. 29, 30</reference>), and so they pray, "Remember not against us our first sins," which some make to look as far back as the golden calf, because God said, <hi type="italic">In the day when I visit I will visit for this sin</hi> of theirs <hi type="italic">upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.32.34">Exod. xxxii. 34</reference>. If the children by repentance and reformation cut off the entail of the parents' sin, they may in faith pray that God will not <hi type="italic">remember them against them.</hi> When God pardons sin he blots it out and remembers it no more. 2. That he would purge away the sins they had been lately guilty of, by the guilt of which their minds and consciences had been defiled: <hi type="italic">Deliver us, and purge away our sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.79.9">v. 9</reference>. Then deliverances from trouble are granted in love, and are mercies indeed, when they are grounded upon the pardon of sin and flow from that; we should therefore be more earnest with God in prayer for the removal of our sins than for the removal of our afflictions, and the pardon of them is the foundation and sweetness of our deliverances. <div eID="gen11925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11926" type="x-p"/> III. They pray that God would work deliverance for them, and bring their troubles to a good end and that speedily: <hi type="italic">Let thy tender mercies speedily prevent us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.79.8">v. 8</reference>. They had no hopes but from God's mercies, his tender mercies; their case was so deplorable that they looked upon themselves as the proper objects of divine compassion, and so near to desperate that, unless divine mercy did speedily interpose to prevent their ruin, they were undone. This whets their importunity: "<hi type="italic">Lord, help us; Lord, deliver us;</hi> help us under our troubles, that we may bear them well; help us out of our troubles, that the spirit may not fail. Deliver us from sin, from sinking." Three things they plead:—1. The great distress they were reduced to: "<hi type="italic">We are brought very low,</hi> and, being low, shall be lost if thou help us not." The lower we are brought the more need we have of help from heaven and the more will divine power be magnified in raising us up. 2. Their dependence upon him: "Thou art the <hi type="italic">God of our salvation,</hi> who alone canst help. <hi type="italic">Salvation belongs to the Lord,</hi> from whom we expect help; for <hi type="italic">in the Lord alone is the salvation of his people.</hi>" Those who make God the God of their salvation shall find him so. 3. The interest of his own honour in their case. They plead no merit of theirs; they pretend to none; but, "<hi type="italic">Help us for the glory of thy name;</hi> pardon us for thy name's sake." The best encouragements in prayer are those that are taken from God only, and those things whereby he has made himself known. Two things are insinuated in this plea:—(1.) That God's name and honour would be greatly injured if he did not deliver them; for those that derided them blasphemed God, as if he were weak and could not help them, or had withdrawn and would not; therefore they plead (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.10">v. 10</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Wherefore should the heathen say, Where is their God?</hi> He has forsaken them, and forgotten them; and this they get by worshipping a God whom they cannot see." (<hi type="italic">Nil præter nubes et c&#339;li numen adorant.</hi> Juv.—<hi type="italic">They adore no other divinity than the clouds and the sky.</hi>) That which was their praise (that they served a God that is every where) was now turned to their reproach and his too, as if they served a God that is nowhere. "Lord," say they, "Make it to appear that thou art by making it to appear that thou art with us and for us, that when we are asked, <hi type="italic">Where is your God?</hi> we may be able to say, He is nigh unto us in all that which we call upon him for, and you see he is so by what he does for us." (2.) That God's name and honour would be greatly advanced if he did deliver them; his mercy would be glorified in delivering those that were so miserable and helpless. By making bare his everlasting arm on their behalf he would make unto himself an everlasting name; and their deliverance would be a type and figure of the great salvation, which in the fulness of time Messiah the Prince would work out, to the glory of God's name. <div eID="gen11926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11927" type="x-p"/> IV. They pray that God would avenge them on their adversaries, 1. For their cruelty and barbarity (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.10">v. 10</reference>): "Let the avenging of our blood" (according to the ancient law, <reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Gen. ix. 6</reference>) "be known among the heathen; let them be made sensible that what judgments are brought upon them are punishments of the wrong they have done to us; let this be in our sight, and by this means <hi type="italic">let God be known among the heathen</hi> as <hi type="italic">the God to whom vengeance belongs</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.1">Ps. xciv. 1</reference>) and the God that espouses his people's cause." Those that have intoxicated themselves with the blood of the saints shall have <hi type="italic">blood given them to drink,</hi> for they are worthy. 2. For their insolence and scorn (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Render to them their reproach.</hi> The indignities which by word and deed they have done to the people of God himself and his name let them be repaid to them with interest." The reproach wherewith men have reproached us only we must leave it to God whether he will render to them or no, and must pray that he would forgive them; but the reproach wherewith they have blasphemed God himself we may in faith pray that God would render seven-fold into their bosoms, so as to strike at their hearts, to humble them, and bring them to repentance. This prayer is a prophecy, of the same import with that of Enoch, that God will convince sinners of all their hard speeches which they have spoken against him (<reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>) and will return them into their own bosoms by everlasting terrors at the remembrance of them. <div eID="gen11927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11928" type="x-p"/> V. They pray that God would find out a way for the rescue of his poor prisoners, especially the condemned prisoners, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.11">v. 11</reference>. The case of their brethren who had fallen into the hands of the enemy was very sad; they were kept close prisoners, and, because they durst not be heard to bemoan themselves, they vented their griefs in deep and silent sighs. All their breathing was sighing, and so was their praying. They were appointed to die, as sheep for the slaughter, and had received the sentence of death within themselves. This deplorable case the psalmist recommends, 1. To the divine pity: "<hi type="italic">Let their sighs come up before thee,</hi> and be thou pleased to take cognizance of their moans." 2. To the divine power: "<hi type="italic">According to the greatness of thy arm,</hi> which no creature can contest with, <hi type="italic">preserve thou those that are appointed to die</hi> from the death to which they are appointed." Man's extremity is God's opportunity to appear for his people. See <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.8-2Cor.1.10">2 Cor. i. 8-10</reference>. <div eID="gen11928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11929" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> They promise the returns of praise for the answers of prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">So we will give thee thanks for ever.</hi> Observe, 1. How they please themselves with their relation to God. "Though we are oppressed and brought low, yet we are the sheep of thy pasture, not disowned and cast off by thee for all this: <hi type="italic">We are thine; save us.</hi>" 2. How they promise themselves an opportunity of praising God for their deliverance, which they <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> desired, and would bid welcome, because it would furnish them with matter for thanksgiving and put their hearts in tune for that excellent work, the work of heaven. 3. How they oblige themselves not only to give God thanks at present, but to <hi type="italic">show forth his praise unto all generations,</hi> that is, to do all they could both to perpetuate the remembrance of God's favours to them and to engage their posterity to keep up the work of praise. 4. How they plead this with God: "Lord, appear for us against our enemies; for, if they get the better, they will <hi type="italic">blaspheme thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.12">v. 12</reference>); but, if we be delivered, we will praise thee. Lord, we are that people of thine which thou hast <hi type="italic">formed for thyself, to show forth thy praise;</hi> if we be cut off, whence shall that rent, that tribute, be raised?" Note, Those lives that are entirely devoted to God's praise are assuredly taken under his protection.  <chapter eID="Ps.79"/> <div eID="gen11929" type="x-p"/>

entries.aa24cfc73fc852d7dd412a01c89e3594afd4e223: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6419"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 79</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.79.1-Ps.79.13">Psa 79:1-13</reference>. Though we deserve much, do not the heathen deserve more for their violence to us (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.3-Jer.51.5">Jr 51:3-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.1.14">Zec 1:14</reference>)? The singular denotes the chief power, and the use of the plural indicates the combined confederates.<div eID="gen9835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9836" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">called upon--</hi>or, "by"<div eID="gen9836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy name--</hi>proclaimed Thy attributes and professed allegiance (<reference osisRef="Isa.12.4">Is 12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.21">Ac 2:21</reference>). <div eID="gen9837" type="x-p"/>

entries.c834306bd92a5ba1b016fa8ddf495bffae8598b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6425"/><div sID="gen9840" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6425"/><hi type="bold">9. for ... glory of thy name [and for] thy name's sake--</hi>both mean for illustrating Thy attributes, faithfulness, power, &c.<div eID="gen9840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9841" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purge ... sins--</hi>literally, "provide atonement for us." Deliverance from sin and suffering, for their good and God's glory, often distinguish the prayers of Old Testament saints (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>). <div eID="gen9841" type="x-p"/>

This ground of pleading often used (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.12">Ex 32:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.14.13-Num.14.16">Nu 14:13-16</reference>).<div eID="gen9842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blood ... shed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.79.3">Psa 79:3</reference>). <div eID="gen9843" type="x-p"/>
entries.deeea64bfeb2155b69b9d2cee90a09b5f132423a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6427"/><div sID="gen9844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6427"/><hi type="bold">11. prisoner--</hi>the whole captive people.<div eID="gen9844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">power--</hi>literally, "arm" (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.15">Psa 10:15</reference>). <div eID="gen9845" type="x-p"/>
entries.c88ff554edfdb20cc6b4fb8f56c8b7cd9413cf19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6428"/><div sID="gen9846" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6428"/><hi type="bold">12. into their bosom--</hi>The lap or folds of the dress is used by Eastern people for receiving articles. They reproached God as well as His people. <div eID="gen9846" type="x-p"/>

entries.2f042f31be84d162aea9076069223938d12ac0c0: <div eID="gen21175" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21176" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21177" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21177" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21176" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21178" type="x-p"/> The psalmist complains of the cruelty of his enemies and the desolations of Jerusalem, and prays against them, <reference osisRef="Psa.79.1-Psa.79.7">Psa 79:1-7</reference>. He prays for the pardon and restoration of his people, and promises gratitude and obedience, <reference osisRef="Psa.79.8-Psa.79.13">Psa 79:8-13</reference>. <div eID="gen21178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21179" type="x-p"/> The title, A Psalm of Asaph, must be understood as either applying to a person of the name of Asaph who lived under the captivity; or else to the family of Asaph; or to a band of singers still bearing the name of that Asaph who flourished in the days of David; for most undoubtedly the Psalm was composed during the Babylonish captivity, when the city of Jerusalem lay in heaps, the temple was defiled, and the people were in a state of captivity. David could not be its author. Some think it was composed by Jeremiah; and it is certain that the sixth and sevenths verses are exactly the same with <reference osisRef="Jer.10.25">Jer 10:25</reference> : "Pour out thy fury upon the heathen that know thee not, and upon the families that call not on thy name: for they have eaten up Jacob, and devoured him, and consumed him; and have made his habitation desolate." <div eID="gen21179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21180" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21181" type="x-p"/> The heathen are come into thine inheritance - Thou didst cast them out, and take thy people in; they have cast us out, and now taken possession of the land that belongs to thee. They have defiled the temple, and reduced Jerusalem to a heap of ruins; and made a general slaughter of thy people.
entries.5cd3097ea1aaa3ac45b6780a1a9715da89e3b6ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21182" type="x-p"/> The dead bodies of thy servants - It appears that in the destruction of Jerusalem the Chaldeans did not bury the bodies of the slain, but left them to be devoured by birds and beasts of prey. This was the grossest inhumanity.
entries.730a035d5aac906da001323489d5f100fc595984: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21183" type="x-p"/> There was none to bury them - The Chaldeans would not; and the Jews who were not slain were carried into captivity.
entries.0f755779bd462db3ffeda019d449fa21db4e40b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21184" type="x-p"/> We are become a reproach to our neighbors - The Idumeans, Philistines, Phoenicians, Ammonites, and Moabites, all gloried in the subjugation of this people; and their insults to them were mixed with blasphemies against God.
entries.8dbc578261f52483e4d898c858d48d5c7658675f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21185" type="x-p"/> How long, Lord? - Wilt thou continue thine anger against us, and suffer us to be insulted, and thyself blasphemed?
entries.2cfc0884ad72a71222a79ee55bf670402adbf8b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21186" type="x-p"/> Pour out thy wrath - Bad as we are, we are yet less wicked than they. We, it is true, have been unfaithful; but they never knew thy name, and are totally abandoned to idolatry.
entries.ac0ecb0f9718ec420b380458e97a3b63da1e2c00: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21187" type="x-p"/> Laid waste his dwelling-place - The Chaldee understands this of the temple. This, by way of eminence, was Jacob's place. I have already remarked that these two verses are almost similar to <reference osisRef="Jer.10.25">Jer 10:25</reference>, which has led many to believe that Jeremiah was the author of this Psalm.
entries.2c928f51e77338fc62a3db2df68fdee2a1f81fe1: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21188" type="x-p"/> Remember not against us former iniquities - Visit us not for the sins of our forefathers. <div eID="gen21188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21189" type="x-p"/> Speedily prevent us - Let them go before us, and turn us out of the path of destruction; for there is no help for us but in thee. <div eID="gen21189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21190" type="x-p"/> We are brought very low - Literally, "We are greatly thinned." Few of us remain.
entries.a99444431e1c1df16c0b0ec2b40595bd88c01413: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21191" type="x-p"/> Purge away our sins - כפר capper, be propitiated, or receive an atonement (על חטאתינו al chattotheynu) on account of our sins.
entries.6b749d48cd0dec1e348be82d013fa762343dac1b: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21192" type="x-p"/> Where is their God? - Show where thou art by rising up for our redemption, and the infliction of deserved punishment upon our enemies.
entries.c4294c2cc13fb36cd417471dcea2484e43127e5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21193" type="x-p"/> The sighing of the prisoner - The poor captive Israelites in Babylon, who sigh and cry because of their bondage. <div eID="gen21193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21194" type="x-p"/> Those that are appointed to die - בני תמותה beney themuthah, "sons of death." Either those who were condemned to death because of their crimes, or condemned to be destroyed by their oppressors. Both these senses apply to the Israelites: they were sons of death, i.e., worthy of death because of their sins against God; they were condemned to death or utter destruction, by their Babylonish enemies.
entries.38f3a62d4f3af52cdee0aaa15bff0b93718b9ddd: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21195" type="x-p"/> Sevenfold into their bosom - That is, Let them get in this world what they deserve for the cruelties they have inflicted on us. Let them suffer in captivity, who now have us in bondage. Probably this is a prediction.
entries.27b4fb29a3a9b32675b77f9d0759dbac59af9c89: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen21195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21196" type="x-p"/> We thy people - Whom thou hast chosen from among all the people of the earth. <div eID="gen21196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21197" type="x-p"/> And sheep of thy pasture - Of whom thou thyself art the Shepherd. Let us not be destroyed by those who are thy enemies; and we, in all our generations, will give thanks unto thee for ever.  <chapter eID="Ps.79"/> <div eID="gen21197" type="x-p"/>

entries.ac77a80f8bf2db9bd0b7ee8123a3e1130f5453d0: <div eID="gen9804" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Supplicatory Prayer in a Time of Devastation, of Bloodshed, and of Derision</title> <div sID="gen9805" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is in every respect the pendant of Ps 74. The points of contact are not merely matters of style (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.79.5">Psa 79:5</reference>, <hi type="italic">how long for ever</hi>? with <reference osisRef="Ps.74.1">Psa 74:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.10">Psa 74:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.79.10">Psa 79:10</reference>, יוּדע, with <reference osisRef="Ps.74.5">Psa 74:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.79.2">Psa 79:2</reference>, the giving over to the wild beasts, with <reference osisRef="Ps.74.19">Psa 74:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.14">Psa 74:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.79.13">Psa 79:13</reference>, the conception of Israel as of a flock, in which respect <reference osisRef="Ps.79.1-Ps.79.13">Psa 79:1-13</reference> is judiciously appended to <reference osisRef="Ps.78.70-Ps.78.72">Psa 78:70-72</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ps.74.1">Psa 74:1</reference>, and also with <reference osisRef="Ps.74.19">Psa 74:19</reference>). But the mutual relationships lie still deeper. Both Psalms have the same Asaphic stamp, both stand in the same relation to Jeremiah, and both send forth their complaint out of the same circumstances of the time, concerning a destruction of the Temple and of Jerusalem, such as only the age of the Seleucidae (1 Macc. 1:31; 3:45, 2 Macc. 8:3) together with the Chaldaean period<note placement="foot">According to <hi type="italic">Sofrim</hi> xviii. §3, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.1-Ps.79.13">Psa 79:1-13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.137.1-Ps.137.9">Psa 137:1-9</reference> are the Psalms for the Kînoth-day, i.e., the 9th day of Ab, the day commemorative of the Chaldaean and Roman destruction of Jerusalem.</note> can exhibit, and in conjunction with a defiling of the Temple and a massacre of the servants of God, of the <hi type="italic">Chasîdîm</hi> (1 Macc. 7:13, 2 Macc. 14:6), such as the age of the Seleucidae exclusively can exhibit. The work of the destruction of the Temple which was in progress in Ps 74, appears in <reference osisRef="Ps.79.1-Ps.79.13">Psa 79:1-13</reference> as completed, and here, as in the former Psalm, one receives the impression of the outrages, not of some war, but of some persecution: it is straightway the religion of Israel for the sake of which the sanctuaries are destroyed and the faithful are massacred. <div eID="gen9805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9806" type="x-p"/> Apart from other striking accords, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.6-Ps.79.7">Psa 79:6-7</reference> are repeated verbatim in Jer 10:25. It is in itself far more probable that Jeremiah here takes up the earlier language of the Psalm than that the reverse is the true relation; and, as Hengstenberg has correctly observed, this is also favoured by the fact that the words immediately before viz., <reference osisRef="Jer.10.24">Jer 10:24</reference>, originate out of <reference osisRef="Ps.6.2">Psa 6:2</reference>, and that the connection in the Psalm is a far closer one. But since there is no era of pre-Maccabaean history corresponding to the complaints of the Psalm,<note placement="foot">Cassiodorus and Bruno observe: <hi type="italic">deplorat Antiochi persecutionem tempore Machabeorum factam, tunc futuram</hi>. And Notker adds: To those who have read the First Book of the Maccabees it (viz., the destruction bewailed in the Psalm) is familiar.</note> <div eID="gen9806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9807" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah is to be regarded in this instance as the example of the psalmist; and in point of fact the borrower is betrayed in <reference osisRef="Ps.79.6-Ps.79.7">Psa 79:6-7</reference> of the Psalm by the fact that the correct על of Jeremiah is changed into אל, the more elegant משׁפחות into ממלכות, and the plural אכלוּ into אכל, and the soaring exuberance of Jeremiah’s expression is impaired by the omission of some of the words.
entries.877a0b745bb630c559b42e77bafd9920616a092e: <reference osisRef="Ps.79.1-Ps.79.4">Psa 79:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen9807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9808" type="x-p"/> The Psalm begins with a plaintive description, and in fact one that makes complaint to God. Its opening sounds like Lam 1:10. The defiling does not exclude the reducing to ashes, it is rather spontaneously suggested in <reference osisRef="Ps.74.7">Psa 74:7</reference> in company with wilful incendiarism. The complaint in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.79.1">Psa 79:1</reference></hi> reminds one of the prophecy of Micah, Mic 3:12, which in its time excited so much vexation (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.18">Jer 26:18</reference>); and <reference osisRef="Ps.79.2">Psa 79:2</reference>, Deu 28:26. עבדיך confers upon those who were massacred the honour of martyrdom. The lxx renders לעיים by εἰς ὀπωροφυλάκιον, a flourish taken from Isa 1:8. Concerning the quotation from memory in 1 Macc. 7:16f., vid., the introduction to Ps 74. The translator of the originally Hebrew First Book of the Maccabees even in other instances betrays an acquaintance with the Greek Psalter (cf. 1 Macc. 1:37, καὶ ἐξέχεαν αἷμα ἀθῷον κύκλῳ τοῦ ἁγιάσματος). “As water,” i.e., (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.15.23">Deu 15:23</reference>) without setting any value upon it and without any scruple about it. <reference osisRef="Ps.44.14">Psa 44:14</reference> is repeated in Psa 79:4. At the time of the Chaldaean catastrophe this applied more particularly to the Edomites.
entries.72a5e25d232aca42dd05d20a60ddaa141c1958b7: <reference osisRef="Ps.79.5-Ps.79.8">Psa 79:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen9808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9809" type="x-p"/> Out of the plaintive question how long? and whether endlessly God would be angry and cause His jealousy to continue to burn like a fire (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.22">Deu 32:22</reference>), grows up the prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.6">Psa 79:6</reference>) that He would turn His anger against the heathen who are estranged from the hostile towards Him, and of whom He is now making use as a rod of anger against His people. The taking over of <reference osisRef="Ps.79.6-Ps.79.7">Psa 79:6-7</reference> from <reference osisRef="Jer.10.25">Jer 10:25</reference> is not betrayed by the looseness of the connection of thought; but in themselves these four lines sound much more original in Jeremiah, and the style is exactly that of this prophet, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.6.11">Jer 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.3">Jer 2:3</reference>, and frequently, Psa 49:20. The אל, instead of על, which follows שׁפך is incorrect; the singular אכל gathers all up as in one mass, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Isa 5:26</reference>; Isa 17:13. The fact that such power over Israel is given to the heathen world has its ground in the sins of Israel. From <reference osisRef="Ps.79.8">Psa 79:8</reference> it may be inferred that the apostasy which raged earlier is now checked. ראשׁנים is not an adjective (<reference osisRef="Job.31.28">Job 31:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.2">Isa 59:2</reference>), which would have been expressed by עונותינו חראשׁנים, but a genitive: the iniquities of the forefathers (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.14">Lev 26:14</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1-Ps.39.13">Psa 39:1-13</reference>). On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.79.8">Psa 79:8</reference></hi> of Jdg 6:6. As is evident from <reference osisRef="Ps.79.9">Psa 79:9</reference>, the poet does not mean that the present generation, itself guiltless, has to expiate the guilt of the fathers (on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Deut.24.16">Deu 24:16</reference>; 2Ki 14:6; <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.20">Eze 18:20</reference>); he prays as one of those who have turned away from the sins of the fathers, and who can now no longer consider themselves as placed under wrath, but under sin-pardoning and redeeming grace.
entries.e0e1e913aa9be4f7da6601fa49df3ee169a8173b: <reference osisRef="Ps.79.9-Ps.79.12">Psa 79:9-12</reference> <div eID="gen9809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9810" type="x-p"/> The victory of the world is indeed not God’s aim; therefore His own honour does not suffer that the world of which He has made use in order to chasten His people should for ever haughtily triumph. שׁמך is repeated with emphasis at the end of the petition in <reference osisRef="Ps.79.9">Psa 79:9</reference>, according to the figure epanaphora. על־דּבר = למען, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.45.5">Psa 45:5</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.7.1">Psa 7:1</reference>, is a usage even of the language of the Pentateuch. Also the motive, “wherefore shall they say?” occurs even in the Tôra (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.12">Exo 32:12</reference>, cf. Num 14:13-17; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.28">Deu 9:28</reference>). Here (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.115.2">Psa 115:2</reference>) it originates out of Joe 2:17. The wish expressed in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.79.10">Psa 79:10</reference></hi> is based upon Deu 32:43. The poet wishes in company with his contemporaries, as eye-witnesses, to experience what God has promised in the early times, viz., that He will avenge the blood of His servants. The petition in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">Deu 32:11</reference> runs like <reference osisRef="Ps.102.21">Psa 102:21</reference>, cf. Psa 18:7. אסיר individualizingly is those who are carried away captive and incarcerated; בּני תמוּתה are those who, if God does not preserve them by virtue of the greatness (גדל, cf. גּדל <reference osisRef="Exod.15.16">Exo 15:16</reference>) of His arm, i.e., of His far-reaching omnipotence, succumb to the power of death as to a <hi type="italic">patria potestas</hi>.<note placement="foot">The Arabic has just this notion in an active application, viz., <hi type="italic">benı̂ el - môt</hi> = the heroes (destroyers) in the battle.</note> <div eID="gen9810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9811" type="x-p"/> That the petition in <reference osisRef="Ps.79.12">Psa 79:12</reference> recurs to the neighbouring peoples is explained by the fact, that these, who might most readily come to the knowledge of the God of Israel as the one living and true God, have the greatest degree of guilt on account of their reviling of God. The bosom is mentioned as that in which one takes up and holds that which is handed to him (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.38">Luk 6:38</reference>); חיק- (על) אל (שׁלּם) השׁיב, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.65.7">Isa 65:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.6">Isa 65:6</reference>; Jer 32:18. A sevenfold requital (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.4.15">Gen 4:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.24">Gen 4:24</reference>) is a requital that is fully carried out as a criminal sentence, for seven is the number of a completed process.
entries.e544f20648407ee095b9cec732c6cfb3e7f67369: <reference osisRef="Ps.79.13">Psa 79:13</reference> <div eID="gen9811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9812" type="x-p"/> If we have thus far correctly hit upon the parts of which the Psalm is composed (9. 9. 9), then the lamentation closes with this tristichic vow of thanksgiving.  <chapter eID="Ps.79"/> <div eID="gen9812" type="x-p"/>

entries.4524643d4393e5b1c86cb58c892a4dc8db37d816:
PSALM 79
This is a complaint and lamentation of the Church when severely afflicted; in which, while the faithful bewail their miserable and, in one sense, undeserved calamities, and accuse their enemies of cruelty, they acknowledge that, in another sense, they have been justly chastised, and humbly betake themselves to the divine mercy. Their confidence of obtaining this, they rest chiefly upon the fact, that they saw God’s dishonor conjoined with their calamities, inasmuch as the ungodly, in oppressing the Church, blasphemed his sacred name.
A Psalm of Asaph.
This psalm, like others, contains internal evidence that it was composed long after the death of David. Some who ascribe it to him allege, in support of this opinion, that the afflictions of the Church have been here predicted by the spirit of prophecy, to encourage the faithful in bearing the cross when these afflictions should arrive. But there does not appear to be any ground for such a supposition. It is not usual with the prophets thus to speak historically in their prophecies. Whoever judiciously reflects upon the scope of the poem will easily perceive that it was composed either when the Assyrians, after having burnt the temple, and destroyed the city, dragged the people into captivity, or when the temple was defiled by Antiochus, after he had slaughtered a vast number of the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Its subject agrees very well with either of these periods. Let us then take it as an admitted point, that this complaint was dictated to the people of God at a time when the Church was subjected to oppression, and when matters were reduced to the most hopeless condition. How cruelly the Assyrians conducted themselves is well known. And under the tyranny of Antiochus, if a man dared simply to open his mouth in defense of the pure worship of God, he did it at the risk of immediately forfeiting his life.
Psalm 79:1-4
1. O God! the heathen [or the nations] have come into thy inheritance; they have defiled the temple of thy holiness; they have laid Jerusalem in heaps. 2. They have given the dead bodies of thy servants for food to the fowls of the heaven; the flesh of thy meek ones to the beasts of the earth. 3. They have shed their blood like water, around Jerusalem: and there was none to bury them. 4. We have been a reproach to our neighbors; a scorn and a derision to them that are around us.
 
1. O God! the heathen have come into thy inheritance. Here the prophet, in the person of the faithful, complains that the temple was defiled, and the city destroyed. In the second and third verses, he complains that the saints were murdered indiscriminately, and that their dead bodies were cast forth upon the face of the earth, and deprived of the honor of burial. Almost every word expresses the cruelty of these enemies of the Church. When it is considered that God had chosen the land of Judea to be a possession to his own people, it seemed inconsistent with this choice to abandon it to the heathen nations, that they might ignominiously trample it under foot, and lay it waste at their pleasure. The prophet, therefore, complains that when the heathen came into the heritage of God, the order of nature was, as it were, inverted. The destruction of the temple, of which he speaks in the second clause, was still less to be endured; for thus the service of God on earth was extinguished, and religion destroyed. He adds, that Jerusalem, which was the royal seat of God, was reduced to heaps. By these words is denoted a hideous overthrow. The profanation of the temple, and the destruction of the holy city, involving, as they did, heaven-daring impiety, which ought justly to have provoked the wrath of God against these enemies — the prophet begins with them, and then comes to speak of the slaughter of the saints. The atrocious cruelty of these persecutions is pointed out from the circumstance that they not only put to death the servants of God, but also exposed their dead bodies to the beasts of the field, and to birds of prey, to be devoured, instead of burying them. Men have always had such a sacred regard to the burial of the dead, as to shrink from depriving even their enemies of the honor of sepulture.
If this psalm was written on the taking of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, or during the Babylonish captivity, it would appear, from this verse, that when the Chaldeans destroyed Jerusalem, they left the bodies of the slain unburied, to be devoured by beasts and birds of prey.
Whence it follows, that those who take a barbarous delight in seeing the bodies of the dead torn to pieces and devoured by beasts, more resemble these savage and cruel animals than human beings. It is also shown that these persecutors acted more atrociously than enemies ordinarily do, inasmuch as they made no more account of shedding human blood than of pouring forth water. From this we learn their insatiable thirst for slaughter. When it is added, there was none to bury them, this is to be understood as applying to the brethren and relatives of the slain. The inhabitants of the city were stricken with such terror by the indiscriminate butchery perpetrated by these ruthless assassins upon all who came in their way, that no one dared to go forth. God having intended that, in the burial of men, there should be some testimony to the resurrection at the last day, it was a double indignity for the saints to be despoiled of this right after their death. But it may be asked, Since God often threatens the reprobate with this kind of punishment, why did he suffer his own people to be devoured of beasts? We must remember, what we have stated elsewhere, that the elect, as well as the reprobate, are subjected to the temporal punishments which pertain only to the flesh. The difference between the two cases lies solely in the issue; for God converts that which in itself is a token of his wrath into the means of the salvation of his own children. The same explanation, then, is to be given of their want of burial which is given of their death. The most eminent of the servants of God may be put to a cruel and ignominious death — a punishment which we know is often executed upon murderers, and other despisers of God; but still the death of the saints does not cease to be precious in his sight: and when he has suffered them to be unrighteously persecuted in the flesh, he shows, by taking vengeance on their enemies, how dear they were to him. In like manner, God, to stamp the marks of his wrath on the reprobate, even after their death, deprives them of burial; and, therefore, he threatens a wicked king, “He shall be buried with the burial of all ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem,” (Jeremiah 22:19; see also Jeremiah 36:30.)
Similar threatenings are to be found in Isaiah 14:19, 20; Jeremiah 8:2.
When he exposes his own children to the like indignity, he may seem for a time to have forsaken them; but he afterwards converts it into the means of furthering their salvation; for their faith, being subjected to this trial, acquires a fresh triumph. When in ancient times the bodies of the dead were anointed, that ceremony was performed for the sake of the living whom they left behind them, to teach them, when they saw the bodies of the dead carefully preserved, to cherish in their hearts the hope of a better life. The faithful, then, by being deprived of burial, suffer no loss, when they rise by faith above these inferior helps, that they may advance with speedy steps to a blessed immortality.
